transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-08
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~63 min
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), John Rivera (CTO - Vela), Linda Park (SRE - Vela), Evan Li (Platform Eng - Vela)

Summary:
Short: deep dive into p95/p99 tail latency issues we've seen in Vela's inference pipeline, focusing on streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache behavior, batching, quantization, and network hop implications for their private deployment. Agreed to share detailed traces and run an on-prem pilot.

Topics covered:
- p95 / p99 characterization and measurement
- streaming vs non-streaming request paths
- KV cache hit/miss behavior and eviction patterns
- batching (adaptive / continuous batching) and its impact on tail latency
- quantization/FP16 vs int8 latency vs accuracy tradeoffs
- VPC/on-prem network hops, envoy/proxy impact, and TCP warmup
- rollout plan: pilot + benchmarks + pricing

Action items (captured here and in metadata): see action_items field above

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, John, Linda, Evan, appreciate you making time. We wanted to do a focused run through of the p95/p99 tail issues you flagged in the ticket. Maya from our infra team is here to run through traces.

[00:22] John (CTO): Thanks Alex. Yeah we're seeing spikes in p99 around 450-600ms for short requests that should be 120-160ms. p95 is okay-ish around 180-220ms but the tail is killing us. We suspect something in our on-prem networking or maybe kv-cache thrash.

[00:41] Maya (SE): Cool. Quick agenda: 1) align on measurement methodology so p95/p99 are comparable, 2) look at traces (client->ingress->model), 3) KV cache & batching behavior, 4) quantization impact, 5) recommendations.

[01:05] Linda (SRE): Quick note: we run a VPC private deployment with the Redwood control plane but traffic exits through our internal NAT; we also have an envoy sidecar on each node. Could that be a source?

[01:18] Maya: Yes envoy and extra hops can add tail. We'll show how additional 1-2 ms per hop aggregates under retries and cold keys. Also need to check TCP connection reuse and TLS session caching.

[02:05] Alex: Before we jump into traces can you confirm your client mix? short prompts vs long prompts, streaming enabled?

[02:15] Evan (Platform Eng): Majority are short prompts, ~85% under 80 tokens. We have two routes: streaming enabled for interactive UI, and non-streaming for batch scoring. The spikes are mostly on the streaming route.

[02:40] Maya: Streaming vs non-streaming is a huge difference. With streaming we flush tokens as they're generated and network framing interacts with small writes. If there's head-of-line blocking in envoy it can blow up p99.

[03:12] [showing trace] Maya: Here's a p99 trace from last Friday. Notice the pattern: fast decode time on GPU (~10ms), then a long pause ~300-400ms where request is stuck in the ingress.

[03:33] John: That ingress pause correlates with a work-queue backlog we saw on the host. Might be CPU pressure from other containers.

[03:45] Maya: Right, and also we see KV cache misses on the same requests. Misses cause full model forward passes rather than cheap KV pops.

[04:12] Linda: Our cache size is set conservatively low because of memory limits; eviction policy is LRU. Maybe too aggressive.

[04:30] Maya: If your KV cache hit rate is low for short prompt prefixes, p99 will spike because a cold key forces the longer path. We recommend sampling hit rates by route and by user-id.

[05:02] Alex: For batch behavior, are you using Redwood's continuous batching or fixed micro-batching inside the runtime?

[05:10] Evan: We initially used fixed batch windows on our side, but switched to Redwood continuous batching when we onboarded. Not sure if config is tuned.

[05:25] Maya: Continuous batching tries to trade latency for throughput; default max wait is 20ms, but under bursty traffic it can create queueing that inflates p99. You can tighten batching latency SLOs or enable dynamic burst thresholds.

[06:05] [10:00 marker - mid-discussion] Maya: There's also the quantization angle. If you run int8 kernels you can get 20-30% latency wins per token, but first-token decode sometimes adds overhead for kernel init—so warmup is important.

[06:32] John: We're using an FP16 variant in prod to be safer on quality. Would int8 be safe for our instructions model?

[06:45] Maya: We'll provide a quantization report. In lab int8 on similar models to yours dropped latency 18-27% while maintaining BLEU/EM metrics within acceptable bounds, but we always recommend per-customer evals.

[07:12] Alex: Let's walk through a concrete example: short prompt, streaming path, 1-2 network hops through envoy, cache miss, continuous batching 20ms max wait, FP16 model. Approx compute time on GPU ~12ms. Where does the 400ms come from?

[07:34] Maya: The biggest suspect is queuing at ingress + TCP/TLS handshake + sidecar instabilities. In one trace we saw socket reuse failing and a 250ms TLS renegotiation because session cache was cold.

[07:56] Linda: Ah, we do rotate some containers frequently for CI. That could cause TCP pools to drain.

[08:10] Evan: Also curious about our KV cache hot-keying; a few users have super high fanout and evict their own keys.

[08:25] Maya: Hot-keying leads to thrash: one user can evict others and cause sequential cache misses which hurt p99. We suggested sharded KV caches per-customer or TTL bumping for high-frequency keys.

[09:05] [12:30 marker] Alex: On the Redwood side we can instrument per-route kv hit rate and expose it in the console; we'll send you the queries.

[09:18] Maya: We also saw that while streaming, small writes are coalesced differently by the OS. If envoy is running with default flushing parameters, you get Nagle-ish delays. Tunables exist (TCP_NODELAY, write coalescing).

[09:44] John: So actionables: check TLS reuse, enable TCP_NODELAY between client and envoy, sample kv hit rates, and run a stress test that emulates your short prompt heavy mix.

[10:05] Linda: Agreed. Also we need to quantify network hop latency — internal vs cross-AZ.

[10:20] Maya: For cross-AZ, even 2-3 ms per extra hop stacks up with retries and batching. Under 95th percentile it's fine, but p99 shows the cumulative effect.

[10:55] Evan: Let's talk about the pilot: you'd prefer an on-prem pilot to reproduce exact env?

[11:05] Alex: Yes, on-prem pilot with your SREs is recommended. We'll bring a Redwood runtime image, run our tracing harness, and collect p95/p99 across streaming & non-streaming paths. 2-week window is typical.

[11:25] [15:00 marker - looking at batching traces] Maya: Here's a heatmap: when throughput dips, the batching window waits the full 20ms, but when bursts happen we hit max batch size and processing spikes — that creates stragglers that increase p99.

[11:52] John: Is there an option to prioritize small requests?

[12:00] Maya: Yes, you can do size-based prioritization or route tagging to steer small-latency SLO traffic to instances with lower batching settings, or run a dedicated pool for low-latency interactive traffic.

[12:28] Linda: Dedicated pool sounds interesting but adds cost. We'll need to compare unit economics.

[12:40] Alex: Redwood Optimize can produce cost vs tail-latency curves; we'll share a sample report from a similar customer.

[13:10] [20:00 marker] Maya: On quantization warmups: int8 kernels often JIT/prepare the per-layer scales and a small kernel init happens on first use — we can pre-warm on deploy to avoid first-request penalties.

[13:36] Evan: How big of an impact is that init?

[13:42] Maya: Maybe 30-70ms on first few requests depending on model architecture; negligible after warmup. For streaming first-token penalties can be visible, so pre-warm or run synthetic warmup traffic.

[14:00] John: Regarding monitoring, can we get alerting specifically on tail latency regressions tied to kv hit-rate drops?

[14:12] Maya: Yes, set an alert on p99 spike and correlate with kv hit-rate. We can add a derived metric: p99_when_kv_miss to help.

[14:41] Linda: We also want to see per-route TLS session reuse metrics and envoy queue lengths.

[14:50] Maya: We'll add those to the runbook.

[15:05] Alex: Let's review the proposed pilot steps and responsibilities.

[15:15] Maya: Step 1: Redwood runs tracing harness in your env (needs access to test cluster). Step 2: SREs run traffic profile for 48-72 hours, capturing streaming and non-streaming. Step 3: We run quantization A/Bs in a staging runtime and share delta impacts. Step 4: If results good, config changes and a short reserve for Dedicated pool.

[15:43] John: Sounds good. Cost question: if we do a dedicated pool for low-latency traffic, how do we size it?

[15:53] Alex: We'll provide sizing guidance based on p95 throughput targets and model token/sec. Dedicated reserved capacity pricing will be in the follow-up.

[16:10] Evan: One more nuance: some of our clients have bursty short sessions followed by quiet tails — that pattern causes queuing. Any suggestions?

[16:22] Maya: Consider adaptive batching with a time cap and a token cap, plus a small pre-allocated warm pool to absorb spikes. Also prefix caching for frequent prompts helps.

[16:39] [closing discussion] Alex: To recap: 1) We'll send runbook and raw trace ingestion scripts; 2) Maya will prepare quantization tradeoffs + warmup guidance; 3) Vela will share traffic shapes and allow a 2-week on-prem pilot; 4) Redwood will send Dedicated sizing & pricing.

[16:59] John: Thanks, that captures it. We'll start collecting traces and open ticket with creds for your test harness.

[17:12] Linda: We'll also try enabling TCP_NODELAY and check envoy configs this week and report back.

[17:28] Alex: Great. Anyone else have lingering questions?

[17:35] Evan: Not from me. Appreciate the detail.

[17:45] Alex: Thanks all. We'll follow up by email with artifacts.

[17:51] John: Thanks.

[18:00] Call ends.
